query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A moderate isothermal annealing treatment at a temperature of Tg–30 K for 10 minutes applied to a rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 high-entropy alloy will promote atomic relaxation and homogenize the phosphorus distribution, thereby increasing the thermal stability of the amorphous state and widening the supercooled liquid region by approximately 10–20% relative to the as-quenched material.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 high-entropy alloy produced by rapid cooling (e.g., via melt-spinning) that exhibits an amorphous microstructure with localized regions of phosphorus enrichment.
generation.intervention: Perform an isothermal annealing treatment at Tg–30 K for 10 minutes in an inert (argon) atmosphere.
generation.conditions: The treatment must be conducted well below the crystallization onset temperature (e.g., below ~1200 K) and in an oxygen-free environment to prevent oxidation. The 10-minute duration is chosen based on preliminary relaxation observations in similar systems to allow sufficient atomic diffusion without triggering crystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic mobility at sub-Tg temperatures facilitates the redistribution of phosphorus atoms, eliminating local heterogeneities that act as nucleation sites for crystallization.
generation.mechanism: Controlled thermal energy during sub-Tg annealing promotes the relaxation of internal stresses and a uniform distribution of phosphorus, thereby increasing the nucleation barrier for crystallization and stabilizing the amorphous network.
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed samples will exhibit an increased width of the supercooled liquid region (ΔT increased by 10–20%) and a higher onset temperature of crystallization compared to the as-quenched baseline, indicating improved thermal stability.
generation.baseline: A rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy produced by melt-spinning without any post-quench annealing.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is confined to short annealing durations at temperatures safely below Tg; prolonged annealing or a temperature above Tg may lead to undesirable crystallization.
generation.uncertainty: While the short-duration annealing is expected to improve homogeneity, uncertainties remain concerning the optimal time-temperature regime for maximum benefit and the potential impact on mechanical properties such as ductility. However, the sub-Tg approach has been validated in similar glass systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy ribbons. Subject one set to isothermal annealing at Tg–30 K for 10 minutes under argon, and leave the other set unannealed. Use DSC and XRD to compare the width of the supercooled liquid region and detect any signs of crystallization.
measurements: DSC analysis to determine Tg, Tx, and ΔT (supercooled liquid region width)
XRD to confirm the amorphous structure and check for emergent crystalline peaks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed sample shows no statistically significant increase in ΔT or exhibits signs of crystallization compared to the as-quenched sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The cooling profile recorded during welding (at a cooling rate of 154 K/s) demonstrates that the Cantor alloy solidifies at a temperature of 1478 K []. Previous studies reported its melting temperatures as 1607 K [,], 1523 K [], and 1543 K [], indicating a relatively narrow range of solidification. In contrast, the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy containing phosphorus exhibits a significantly broader solidification temperature range and more complex crystallization behavior. Pronounced thermal effects were observed at T3 = 1291 K and T4 = 1206 K during slow cooling on a copper plate (52 K/s), and at T3 = 977 K and T4 = 960 K during rapid cooling following a brief electric arc pulse (3018 K/s). This marked reduction in solidification temperatures compared to the Cantor alloy demonstrates the role of phosphorus in modifying thermal behavior and promoting amorphization. These results highlight the critical importance of controlling cooling rates and alloy composition to optimize phase stability and microstructure. papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.system: A high-entropy alloy system based on Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni with a phosphorus content (P20) added to the conventional Cantor alloy composition.
papers.approach: The study varied cooling rates—from slow cooling (approximately 52 K/s, using a copper plate) to rapid cooling (via a brief electric arc pulse at ~3018 K/s, and melt-spinning)—to examine the effect of phosphorus on the solidification behavior, amorphization, and phase formation.
papers.findings: Phosphorus addition leads to a significantly broader solidification temperature range with distinct crystallization events (e.g., thermal effects at ~1291 K and ~1206 K under slow cooling, and further reduced temperatures under rapid cooling). Very rapid cooling (melt-spinning) resulted in an amorphous structure as verified by XRD and TEM. The alloy’s thermal behavior indicates that phosphorus enhances glass-forming ability when cooling rates are sufficiently high.
papers.mechanism: Phosphorus is proposed to modify the crystallization pathway by promoting the formation of phosphide-rich phases (or influencing eutectic systems) and reducing the effective solidification temperature of primary phases. This may lower the nucleation barrier for amorphization and lead to a kinetically stabilized amorphous state.

papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl (Introduction portion)
papers.system: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys, with reference to Ni-Fe-Cu-P-Si-B glassy systems and NiNbP bulk metallic glasses.
papers.approach: Comparative discussion based on previous literature that highlights phosphorus’s role in enhancing soft magnetic properties and improving glass-forming ability; the system leverages high mixing entropy combined with phosphorus enrichment.
papers.findings: Prior findings in related phosphorus-containing systems (e.g., NiNbP bulk metallic glasses) indicate that phosphorus addition enhances both hardness and glass-forming ability, albeit sometimes at the cost of reduced ductility.
papers.mechanism: It is suggested that phosphorus contributes to the formation of a stable amorphous phase by increasing the structural disorder and by forming P-rich clusters or phosphide phases that disrupt the regular crystalline nucleation pathways.

established: Phosphorus addition in high-entropy and compositionally complex alloys can significantly enhance glass-forming ability, especially under rapid cooling conditions.
Phosphorus tends to modify the crystallization pathway by broadening the solidification temperature range and promoting the formation of phosphide or eutectic phases.
Previous studies in related systems (e.g., NiNbP bulk metallic glasses) provide supporting evidence that phosphorus enhances hardness and facilitates amorphization.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying cooling rates (slow cooling, rapid arc melting, and melt-spinning) in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
approaches_tried.outcome: Rapid cooling (especially via melt-spinning) effectively produced an amorphous structure, indicating improved glass-forming ability with phosphorus addition, though crystalline phases remain under slower cooling.

mechanisms: Phosphorus lowers the effective solidification temperatures and alters the crystallization pathway by facilitating phosphide or eutectic phase formation.
Enhanced mixing entropy in combination with phosphorus enrichment disrupts crystalline nucleation and promotes a kinetically stabilized amorphous state.
disagreements: While phosphorus improves glass formation and thermal properties, there is concern that it may also reduce ductility or negatively impact toughness in some conditions.
open_questions: What is the optimal phosphorus intervention (in terms of concentration or processing modification) for simultaneously maximizing glass-forming ability and thermal stability without compromising mechanical properties?

How does the interplay between cooling rate, phosphorus content, and other elemental interactions specifically dictate the balance between amorphous phase stability and undesirable crystalline phases?
opportunities: Investigating a single, targeted intervention—such as precise adjustment of phosphorus concentration or its distribution via controlled processing techniques—could optimize the amorphous heat-resistant state.
Combining phosphorus adjustments with tailored rapid cooling protocols might synergistically improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability in otherwise comparable high-entropy systems.
Future work could explore varying levels of phosphorus within a fixed high-entropy matrix to delineate its quantitative impact on critical thermal parameters and mechanical trade-offs.

directions.direction: Tailor the microstructure via post-solidification isothermal annealing to promote structural relaxation and re‐distribution of phosphorus atoms.
directions.type: Heat or thermomechanical treatment and microstructure control
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the improvement of thermal stability by lowering internal energies and eliminating high-energy inhomogeneities that act as crystallization sites. Prior evidence in related metallic glasses (e.g. glass-to-glass transitions, PMC9023469::web::019::4_discussion) supports enhanced stability upon controlled annealing. However, it must be carefully designed so that the annealing temperature is below crystallization.

directions.direction: Increase the cooling rate to an ultra-high value during the quench (e.g., via advanced melt-spinning) to kinetically suppress nucleation of crystals.
directions.assessment: Rapid quenching is known to improve glass-forming ability by bypassing crystalline nucleation. Evidence from phosphorus-containing HEAs shows that rapid cooling (e.g., 3018 K/s in PMC11642357) results in an amorphous structure. The challenge is to balance the extreme cooling rates so that internal stresses are not generated, potentially impairing mechanical properties.

directions.direction: Introduce a minor microalloying addition (e.g., ~2 at% of Nb) to modify the local atomic size distribution and mixing entropy.
directions.assessment: Microalloying can influence the thermodynamics (e.g., liquidus temperature reduction) and disrupt potential heterogeneous nucleation associated with phosphorus clustering. Prior studies in similar glass-forming alloys (see PMC8911233 and PMC7516748 micro-alloying sections) lend support. Feasibility depends on precise compositional control; however, potential trade-offs in ductility must be monitored.

directions.direction: Apply electromagnetic stirring during melting to achieve a more uniform spatial distribution of phosphorus.
directions.assessment: Ensuring uniform distribution of phosphorus is hypothesized to reduce local concentration hotspots that act as nucleation sites. The approach is supported by the idea that composition homogeneity enhances glass-forming ability and thermal stability (e.g., PMC11642357 discussion on phosphorus effects). Practical implementation requires controlled electromagnetic parameters, but it is a promising method to improve amorphous stability.

directions.direction: Introduce an optimized sub‐Tg heat treatment to trigger controlled relaxation of the amorphous state.
directions.assessment: Similar in spirit to the first direction, this narrow treatment window aims to induce structural relaxation without initiating crystallization. Although promising, it may be less direct because it requires fine balancing of temperature and time parameters.
